author_note: Written by an independent AI author given only bench/fresh/BRIEF.md (no code, no rules). Expected outcomes are the author's, unchanged. Author's note: I wrote cases from three viewpoints: a fraudster who knows basic checks exist, an honest but slightly careless vendor in each of the four countries, and a compliance officer. Labels are my own business judgment: harmless formatting differences are approved, gaps the vendor can fix go to the vendor, anything where the payee, tax identity or sender looks like a different party goes to a human reviewer, and a clear sanctions match on the vendor, trade name, tax document or payee is rejected. About a quarter are easy familiar patterns; the rest are boundary dates, related-company documents, contradictory-but-individually-valid details, and alarming-looking honest cases.

cases.title: Uppercase certificate, Pvt. Ltd. with dots
cases.story: Indian vendor typed 'Pvt. Ltd.' with dots; the GST certificate and cheque print the name in capitals as 'PRIVATE LIMITED'. Everything else matches.
cases.why: Capital letters, dots and the spelled-out legal suffix are the same company; all numbers match.

cases.title: German umlauts typed as ue/oe, '&' typed as 'und'
cases.story: German vendor typed its name without umlauts and wrote 'und' instead of '&'; both German-language documents show the official spelling. Numbers all match.
cases.why: ue/oe/ss and 'und' are standard ways of typing the same German name; tax ID and IBAN match.

cases.title: Bank letter exactly 90 days old
cases.story: UK caterer's bank letter is dated exactly 90 days ago. The form says '&' and 'Ltd', the documents say 'and' and 'Limited'.
cases.why: Ninety days is still within the last 90 days, and '&'/'and' plus 'Ltd'/'Limited' are the same name.

cases.title: Garden centre that shares one word with a sanctioned name
cases.story: A UK garden centre is called Blackthorn (a common hedge plant). It has nothing else in common with the sanctioned offshore trading company. Documents are complete and consistent.
cases.why: Sharing one ordinary word with a sanctioned name is not a match; the business is plainly different.

cases.title: US sole proprietor with a DBA on the bank account
cases.story: A US sign maker trades under a business name. The W-9 is in her personal name, and the bank letter shows her name followed by 'DBA' and the business name, exactly as declared on the form.
cases.why: A sole proprietor's account in her own name with her declared trade name is normal and consistent.

form.account_holder: Dana R. Whitfield DBA Whitfield Sign Studio

printed.account_holder: DANA R WHITFIELD DBA WHITFIELD SIGN STUDIO

cases.title: Small Indian shop using a Gmail address
cases.story: A small stationery shop in Chennai gives a Gmail address as its contact and sends a phone photo of a cancelled cheque. Name, GSTIN and account all match.
cases.why: A free email address is normal for a small shop and nothing else is out of line.

cases.title: German UG with the long official suffix
cases.story: A small German software firm typed 'UG'; its documents print 'UG (haftungsbeschränkt)' and write the street name in full. Numbers match.
cases.why: '(haftungsbeschränkt)' is just the full form of the UG suffix and 'Str.' is the usual street abbreviation.

cases.title: Abbreviated address and 'St.' in the name, letter 88 days old
cases.story: UK toolmaker abbreviates its address and writes 'St.' with a dot; documents spell things out. The bank letter is 88 days old.
cases.why: Only punctuation and abbreviations differ, and the letter is inside the 90-day window.

printed.address: Unit 4 Kingsway Trading Estate, St Albans AL1 5UG

cases.title: Name starting with a number, spaced differently
cases.story: Indian LLP writes '3S'; the GST certificate prints '3 S' with a space. Cheque and numbers match.
cases.why: A space between a digit and a letter does not make it a different company.

printed.address: Shed No. 41, Peenya Industrial Area 2nd Phase, Bengaluru 560058

cases.title: Leading 'The' and a comma before Inc.
cases.story: US company typed 'Hawthorne Group Inc'; the W-9 and bank letter say 'The Hawthorne Group, Inc.' Everything else matches.
cases.why: A leading 'The' and punctuation around the suffix are harmless.

printed.address: 250 Civic Center Drive, Suite 500, Columbus, OH 43215

cases.title: Very old German tax certificate, bank letter 89 days old
cases.story: A long-established German haulier sends a tax certificate issued about eight years ago and a bank letter 89 days old, both in German. The form says 'AG', documents say 'Aktiengesellschaft'.
cases.why: Tax registrations do not expire with age; only the bank proof has a 90-day limit and it is met.

cases.title: UK subsidiary whose contact uses the group email domain
cases.story: The UK arm of a foreign group gives a contact whose email is on the parent group's domain. Both documents are in the UK company's own name and all numbers match.
cases.why: A group-wide email domain is common for subsidiaries; the legal entity, tax ID and payee are all the UK company.

printed.address: 7 Bayton Road Industrial Estate, Coventry CV7 9EJ

cases.title: Bank letter 91 days old
cases.story: UK printer's submission is perfect except that the bank letter is dated 91 days ago, one day outside the limit.
cases.why: The bank proof is just past 90 days, so the vendor needs to send a fresh one.

printed.address: Unit 9, Albert Road Works, Bristol BS2 0XJ

cases.title: Same tax certificate uploaded in both slots
cases.story: German cleaning company uploaded its tax certificate twice; the bank-proof slot contains the tax certificate again, so there is no bank document at all.
cases.why: The bank proof is effectively missing because the wrong file was attached; the vendor can simply upload the right one.

cases.title: Vendor's own invoice offered as bank proof
cases.story: US caterer uploaded one of its own invoices, with bank details in the footer, as proof of bank account. The details agree with the form but an invoice is something the vendor wrote itself.
cases.why: An invoice is not issued by the bank, so it proves nothing; the vendor must send a bank letter or cancelled cheque.

cases.title: Wrong entity type picked in the dropdown
cases.story: US corporation whose name and W-9 clearly say 'Inc.' selected 'LLC' in the entity-type dropdown. Everything else is consistent.
cases.why: The entity type contradicts the vendor's own name and tax form, which is a simple dropdown mistake for the vendor to correct.

cases.title: IFSC left blank on the form
cases.story: Indian valve maker left the IFSC field empty on the form. The cancelled cheque shows it, and everything else matches.
cases.why: A required bank field is blank; the vendor should confirm it rather than us filling it in for them.

cases.title: Commercial register extract instead of tax certificate
cases.story: German vendor uploaded its Handelsregisterauszug (company register extract) in the tax slot. It proves the company exists but does not show the VAT number.
cases.why: An official-looking but wrong document; the VAT number is unproven until the vendor sends the tax certificate.

cases.title: Utility bill uploaded as tax proof
cases.story: A UK self-employed bookkeeper uploaded an electricity bill where the VAT certificate should be. Bank letter is fine.
cases.why: A utility bill is not a tax registration; the vendor needs to send the right document.

cases.title: One digit of the account number mistyped on the form
cases.story: Indian vendor mistyped one digit of its account number on the form; the cheque shows the correct number, and the holder name and IFSC match.
cases.why: A single-digit slip with the same holder and bank is a typo the vendor should correct before any payment is set up.

printed.address: Survey No. 88, Balanagar Industrial Estate, Hyderabad 500037

cases.title: W-9 with the tax number box left empty
cases.story: US electrical contractor uploaded a W-9 with name and address filled in but the taxpayer number box blank. The form itself has the EIN typed in.
cases.why: The tax document does not actually show the tax number, so it cannot back up what was typed; the vendor should send a completed W-9.

cases.title: German company with 'United Kingdom' selected as country
cases.story: A German GmbH with a German address, German tax certificate and German bank selected GB in the country dropdown, apparently by mistake.
cases.why: Everything says Germany except the dropdown, so the vendor should correct the country rather than us guessing.

cases.title: Contact email typed with a comma
cases.story: UK upholsterer's contact email has a comma where a dot should be, so it is not a usable address. Documents are fine.
cases.why: We cannot send remittances or queries to an invalid address; the vendor needs to give a working email.

printed.address: Britannia Mills, Colne Road, Huddersfield HD1 3ER

cases.title: No tax certificate uploaded
cases.story: Indian LLP filled in the form and attached a cheque but did not upload any GST certificate.
cases.why: A required document is missing and the vendor can supply it.

cases.title: Bank account belongs to a sister company
cases.story: Indian food company's tax certificate is in its own name, but the cancelled cheque is in the name of a sister company with a similar name, although the form claims the account is the vendor's own.
cases.why: Money would go to a different legal entity than the one we are contracting with, which a person must assess even if the companies are related.

cases.title: Franchisee using the franchisor's VAT registration
cases.story: A UK cleaning franchisee with '(Leeds)' in its name gives the VAT number and certificate of the national franchisor, a separate company at a different address. The bank account is the franchisee's own.
cases.why: The vendor is presenting another company's tax identity as its own; the trailing place name hides that these are two different legal entities.

cases.title: German translation of an existing vendor's name with a lookalike email domain
cases.story: A new German applicant is called 'Nordwind Komponenten GmbH', the German rendering of our existing vendor Northwind Components GmbH, uses 'Northwind Components' as trade name and an email domain almost identical to the real vendor's. Its own documents are internally consistent, with a different VAT number and IBAN.
cases.why: A newly registered entity trading under an existing vendor's name with a near-identical email domain is a classic set-up for diverting that vendor's payments.

cases.title: Different company name, existing vendor's tax number
cases.story: A new US applicant with an unrelated name gives the EIN that already belongs to our existing vendor Summit Office Supplies LLC, on both the form and the W-9. Its bank account is new to us.
cases.why: Two different companies cannot share one tax number, so one of them is borrowing the other's identity.

cases.title: Company asks to be paid into a director's personal account
cases.story: An Indian private limited company names an individual, apparently a director, as the account holder; the cheque is from his personal account. The GST certificate is in the company's name.
cases.why: Paying a company's invoices into a private individual's account is a diversion and tax risk that a person must decide on.

printed.address: 302 Saki Vihar Road, Andheri East, Mumbai 400072

cases.title: Bank letter dated in the future
cases.story: US coatings company's bank letter carries a date six days from now. Everything else matches.
cases.why: A bank cannot issue a letter that has not been written yet, so the document may be fabricated and should not be queried with the sender first.

cases.title: Account holder name pasted over on the bank letter
cases.story: UK marine supplier's bank letter shows the company as account holder, but the PDF reveals the name was pasted over an individual's name. The account number itself was not touched and matches the form.
cases.why: The document was altered to make a personal account look like the company's, which is forgery regardless of the numbers matching.

printed.address: Unit 3, Ocean Quay, Belvidere Road, Southampton SO14 5QY

cases.title: Payments directed to a factoring company
cases.story: German steel fabricator names a factoring company as the account holder and supplies a bank letter in the factor's name. Selling invoices to a factor is a legitimate practice, but the payee is a third party.
cases.why: Paying a third party instead of the vendor needs a person to verify the factoring arrangement independently, even though it is openly declared.

cases.title: New vendor whose contact is an existing vendor's accounts mailbox
cases.story: A new Indian freight company with its own valid documents lists as its contact the accounts email address of our existing vendor Globex Logistics Solutions.
cases.why: Two supposedly independent suppliers sharing one accounts mailbox points to a hidden link, a shell or a compromised mailbox, which a person should look into.

cases.title: Near-match to a sanctioned metals company
cases.story: A US applicant is called 'Orion Vale Metal Recycling Inc'. It shares the two distinctive words and the metals trade with the sanctioned 'Orion Vale Metals LLC', but the name and legal form are not the same. Its documents are consistent.
cases.why: Too close to a sanctioned party in name and trade to pay without a compliance officer checking, but not an outright match that justifies automatic rejection.

cases.title: Existing vendor re-registered with 'London' added and a new bank account
cases.story: Someone applies as 'Brightpath Consulting Ltd London' using the real VAT number and certificate of our existing vendor Brightpath Consulting Ltd, but with a different bank (HSBC instead of Barclays) and an email domain with an added hyphen.
cases.why: This is an existing vendor's identity entering as a 'new' vendor with different bank details and a lookalike email, which sidesteps the normal bank-change checks.

cases.title: Tax number on the form is a completely different valid number from the certificate
cases.story: German parts maker's form shows one valid VAT number while its certificate, in the same company name, shows an entirely different valid VAT number that belongs to another company. This is not a one-digit slip.
cases.why: Two unrelated valid tax numbers for one company cannot be explained as a typo; the certificate may carry someone else's registration.

cases.title: Indian domestic company wants payment to a US bank account in dollars
cases.story: A Chennai software company with an Indian GST registration asks to be paid in USD into an account at Bank of America, giving a SWIFT code and no IFSC. The bank letter is in the company's name.
cases.why: A domestic supplier asking to be paid offshore in a foreign currency raises tax-evasion and money-laundering questions that need a human decision.

printed.address: Tidel Park, 4 Rajiv Gandhi Salai, Taramani, Chennai 600113

cases.title: Contact email domain swaps letters for digits
cases.story: US fastener company's documents are consistent, but the contact email domain spells the company name with the digits '11' in place of the letters 'll'.
cases.why: A real company would not register its own name misspelled with digits; this is the mark of someone impersonating the company by email.

cases.title: Exact sanctions-list name
cases.story: UK applicant's legal name is exactly a sanctioned company. The documents are otherwise in order.
cases.why: The vendor is on the sanctions list.

cases.title: Sanctioned name with a hyphen, a comma and 'Inc.' added
cases.story: US applicant writes its name as 'Meridian-Crest Shipping Co., Inc.'; the W-9 prints it in capitals without punctuation. Underneath the punctuation it is the sanctioned shipping company's name.
cases.why: Punctuation and an extra legal suffix do not change that this is the sanctioned 'Meridian Crest Shipping Co'.

cases.title: Clean vendor, sanctioned alias as the account holder
cases.story: An Indian port agency with a clean name and valid GST certificate asks for payment into an account held by 'MC Shipping', the listed alias of a sanctioned company. The cheque confirms that holder.
cases.why: The money would be paid to a sanctioned party, whatever the name on the vendor record.

cases.title: Sanctioned alias used as the trade name
cases.story: A German GmbH with an innocuous abbreviated legal name declares 'Orion Vale Metallurgy' as its trade name, which is the listed alias of a sanctioned company. Documents are in the legal name.
cases.why: The vendor itself says it trades under a sanctioned party's alias, so it is the sanctioned business under another legal wrapper.

cases.title: Sanctioned name appears only on the tax form
cases.story: A US applicant calls itself 'Vale Industrial Alloys LLC' on the form and bank letter, but the W-9 it uploaded, carrying the same tax number as the form, is in the name of the sanctioned 'Orion Vale Metals LLC'.
cases.why: The taxpayer behind this vendor's own tax number is a sanctioned company, so the friendly name on the form is a front.

cases.title: Sanctioned name reordered with brackets; bank letter gives it away
cases.story: A UK applicant is named 'Blackthorn Trading (Offshore) Limited', the sanctioned name with the words shuffled. Its bank letter shows the account holder as exactly 'Blackthorn Offshore Trading Ltd'.
cases.why: The payee on the bank's own letter is the sanctioned company, and the vendor name is the same words rearranged.
